messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 80
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Asian
  relationship_status: Widowed
  occupation: Coast Guard
  trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another
  pcl5: 64

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Being in Nature: Being in a natural environment similar to where it happened, Future Orientation: Talking about the future, Auditory (Sirens): Sirens
  Maladaptive Strategies: Magical Thinking: I tell myself the event did not really happen or was not that bad, Positive Reframing: I force myself to think only positive thoughts, Thought Suppression: I try to push them out of my mind
  Threat: Avoid Unfamiliar Places: I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger, Risky Behavior: Taking too many risks or doing things that could cause you harm, Safe Seat Seeking: I always choose where to sit based on how safe or protected I feel
  Memory: Fragmented Pieces: My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together, Hard to Recall Deliberately: When I try to deliberately remember what happened I find it difficult to access the memory, Full Sensory Reliving: When the memory comes back it feels completely real across all my senses at once
  Negative Appraisals: Defective Self: There is something wrong with me as a person, Hypervigilance: I have to be on guard all the time, Character Blame: The event happened to me because of the sort of person I am

Vignette:
The accident happened forty-two years ago, during a night rescue off the coast of Alaska. Rajesh was a Chief Petty Officer in the Coast Guard, and that night the sea was a black, pitching wall. A fishing trawler had gone down, and he was on the small boat that reached the survivors first. He remembered the rain, the sirens from the cutter somewhere behind them, and the man in the water—hysterical, flailing. Rajesh reached for him with a hook, the standard tool, but the boat lurched and the hook caught the man not in his life vest but in the soft tissue of his neck. The man did not die, but the injury was severe, and Rajesh saw the blood mixing with the salt spray before the crew hauled him aboard. He never forgot the sound the man made, a wet, surprised cry that sounded, he later thought, like a seal pup. For decades Rajesh told himself it had not really happened that way. He would force his mind to spin the memory into something else—a successful rescue, a grateful handshake—and for a while he believed it. He pushed the images away so hard that his deliberate recall of that night became a jumble of disconnected pieces: the angle of the deck, the colour of the sky, the smell of diesel, but never the whole sequence in order. When the memory came back on its own, however, it was not fragmented. It was complete, across every sense at once—the cold salt on his lips, the siren’s wail, the shock of the hook’s weight in his hand, the warmth of the blood—and he would be right there again, an old man in his living room with his heart pounding and his hands numb.

He came to believe there was something fundamentally wrong with him, not because of what he had done but because of the kind of person he was. A good man would have managed the boat better. A good man would have saved the man cleanly. The event happened to him, he was sure, because he was the sort of person who caused harm. He had to be on guard all the time, even now in his eightieth year, because danger was everywhere and he was the one who missed it. He avoided unfamiliar places because he could not assess the threat in a new environment—too many variables, too many chances to make another mistake. When he did go out, to the grocery store or the VA clinic, he always chose a seat against a wall or in a corner, where no one could approach from behind. At the same time, he took too many risks. He drove without his hearing aids, ignored his doctor’s advice to use a cane, and walked alone on the beach near his retirement condo during storms. He told himself he was not afraid, but the truth was that the risk felt like a familiar companion. If he could control the danger by courting it, he felt less helpless.

His wife had died six years ago, and now his adult children called every Sunday. They talked about the future—their children’s graduations, retirement plans, a trip they wanted him to join. Each time, a cold dread spread through his chest. He did not belong in a future. He had no right to one. He said “maybe” and changed the subject. He had stopped going to the Coast Guard reunions years ago, and his few remaining friends from the service had given up calling. The sirens were the worst. Every time an ambulance passed his building—and it did, several times a day, because he lived near the hospital—his entire body locked. He would freeze, mid-sentence, mid-step, and wait for the world to tilt. It always did, just for a second, before he pushed the thought away again.

What finally brought him to a therapist was his daughter. She had found him standing in his kitchen at three in the morning, fully dressed, staring at a wall. He could not explain why he was there. He had been reliving the hook, the cry, the sirens, and when he came back to himself he was confused about where he was. She begged him to see someone. He agreed because he was tired of telling himself it had not happened. He was tired of being a man who caused harm. What he hoped for, though he could not say it aloud, was to stop feeling like a stranger in his own life. What he feared was that the therapist would confirm what he already knew—that the kind of person he was could not be fixed.
